The trouble is that while we can all agree suffering is bad, we can't agree that it's as bad for everybody else as it is for us. Thought there are also people for whom we think it is worse for them to suffer, than it is for us (children, close family). These sorts of self-sacrificial altruism that we see when a parent sacrifices for a child could be explained in non-religious ways. But it's clear that human beings (albeit probably not consciously) recognize that we are limited in our powers even on the best of days, and even in our own will - we are limited in the extent to which we can do good for others. Could you imagine a world where I did think the suffering of everyone was as bad as it was for my children, my siblings, and myself? Jesus, we'd destroy most human categories of meaning. Most of the compelling human stories have to do with our absolutely disordered moral commitments to a few people.

There is a real point at which moral action begins to impede on the self-interest of the moral agent. Let's say that we saw a person drop something in the street, or saw an old person failing to hail a taxi, and we go help them. Most people will get a sense, driven biologically in part, that they'd done something good. That's likely to carry them through their day (the magnitude and frequency of these acts and their ability to satisfy the person doing them will change with the individual).

If you'd willed that you were going to walk through your section of the city on your way to work and identify every similar sort of good you could accomplish with your time/energy, it would quickly start becoming a bad thing. It might begin to interfere with your own ability to satisfy your needs, say, if you started being late for work regularly. When a person isn't able to prioritize their competitive needs, we find that the damage that can occur in their own personal lives can cause people to become morally worse: resentful, spiteful, passive aggressive, manipulative, etc. Sometimes, the most moral people are the most manipulative when it comes to the satisfactions of their own wants/desires; they feel shame at the power needed to get things for themselves, they sense they are "following all of the rules", and goodness isn't just coming to them.

There is a kind of unarticulated rule in existence that getting a necessary good done for oneself requires a certain selfishness (not necessarily an immoral one), that is to say that you can't always be a "nice guy" (finishing last, blah blah). Being competitive, stating your needs, getting them at the expense of others...these and other competitive, meritocratic systems are in-built with this recognition that many times, the greatest good comes about from everyone pursuing their own goodness, and that the best thing you can do for others is to make them powerful enough to satisfy their own needs.

I think some of the most powerful evil in existence exists in the hearts of some of the nicest and most outwardly moral moral people. Privately they fester in a suffocating resentment of their own lack of will to go get things and prioritize themselves. There is the related argument that the agent with the highest potential for moral actions is also the agent with the most continual situation of self-satisfaction and power. Someone in need has less power to do good than someone with plenty. I'd wager that a wealthy philanthropist can probably do more good (on a power basis per unit time) than 1,000 monks in 1,000 monasteries.

It's typically good for a society to have a certain amount of moral people. They can only tolerate so many perfectly selfish power seekers. Both the most down-and-out (the underman) and the extremes of power represent dangers to a society. And some people use the resentment of the underman to gain their power.

My point is to say that these arguments (those relying on moral action due to some mature recognition that suffering is bad generally) miss the point that suffering is not doled out equally, and it often concentrates where people are least willing to take (at the very least) morally neutral stances, i.e. grades of selfishness. To that, someone might say that our desires are the source of the trouble then. If everyone could just agree to destroy the ego and live like Buddhist monks, nobody would be competing in the rat race.

Of course, that utopian idea of a world monastic community wouldn't work out the way ideologues imagine. Part of what makes this lifestyle significant to Buddhists is just its being contrasted by egoic life. If everybody behaved this way, then this human auto-intoxication with moral guilt would just cause the most moral people to behave with even greater neglect to themselves in a great Ascetic Olympics. Not to mention that if we had all behaved this way, the species probably would have ended many times over within our own history. Additionally, evolution would have probably selected against these sorts of behaviors long ago. The lying, cheating, physically aggressive minority would, like an aggressive tumor in the body, encroach wherever they pleased, creating a power center around which fearful people would surely kneel, long before they knelt to escape Samsara.

Our societies are just as threatened by too much morality as they are by not enough. What happens when a parent acts perfectly moral when they have a child to provide for, in a world with other parents with children to provide for?

The irony is people do believe in Christ because they recognize how the world is. So let's talk about the world the way it is. People appreciate the diffuse concept of good behavior and high ideals depicted in our art, but when it comes to actual sacrifice of individual time/energy/opportunity, we do not apply these things to creating goodness indiscriminately. I think the better part of post-Enlightenment society has realized that optimizing society morally is not enforcing against the ubiquitous self-interested behaviors, but encouraging people to gain in their own power to promote their self-interest.

A world of pure charity and a world of pure barbarism are both equally nonviable. Perfect goodness and perfect evil are the same things, in effect.

I think if you dole out your moral goodness to everyone equally, you aren't noble, you're weak. It's a more beautiful world where a person can "give themselves" to a few, rather than diffusely to the many. Every notion we have of the significance of relationships rests on the fact that we don't care as much about others as we do about that person (or people). When I put a ring on a woman's finger, I'm saying "You and your wellbeing are far more important to me than 99.9999999% of the rest of the world, and I will act at their expense when necessary to make sure you have goodness. Our hates grows because what's really been taken from us is our innate God-given power to decide who and what is morally significant to us. The underlying idea is that the greatest power man has to exert is to decide what he loves and to sacrifice for it. The only thing that could sacrifice for all was Christ himself.

How we negotiate those boundaries is every human being's life battle. I've used examples of innocuous situations, but moral conundrums usually don't apply to picking up objects for people who drop them. Typically moral people are found to do immoral things when it comes to the most high-stakes situations in their lives. All of these discussions of morality as such always fail to acknowledge the concept of significance. If I have 3 children and an unemployed wife at home, is it in my interest to enter the alley at midnight when I hear a woman screaming? Probably not. In stories, our society might praise someone who goes into the alley.
